title: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
summary: Split a search into must-haves applied as non-scoring filters and preferences scored with weighted decay functions, then handle empty results with relaxation ladders and list-wide rules with re-ranking.
outcomes: Explain why must-haves belong in filters and preferences in a score, using the CSP split of hard and preference constraints
Predict how Elasticsearch bool clauses (filter, must, should, must_not) affect matching, scoring and caching
Compute gauss, exp and linear decay scores from origin, offset, scale and decay, and spot the missing-field trap
Build a weighted function_score ranking and explain how phased ranking in Vespa and LinkedIn Recruiter applies it
Design a relaxation ladder for too few results and apply a list-wide constraint with greedy fair re-ranking

lessons.title: Must-haves and nice-to-haves need different machinery

blocks.md:
A recruiter is hiring a senior backend engineer for a hybrid role at a New York office. Some requirements are **must-haves**: the candidate must be authorized to work in the US, and must know Go. Others are **nice-to-haves**: living close to the office, having been active on the platform recently, knowing Kubernetes, and having 8 or more years of experience.

The search engine has to return a ranked list. The question of this course is how to turn these two kinds of requirement into one query that behaves the way the recruiter expects.

Here is a toy pool of 10 candidates that we will use in every lesson. Each row is one fact about each candidate (1 means yes, 0 means no). Distances are kilometers from the office; activity is days since the candidate was last active.

The numbers are invented for teaching, but every score computed from them later in the course is computed exactly with the Elasticsearch formulas.

blocks.title: The toy candidate pool and its two hard constraints

scenes.caption: Ten candidates. Ines has no location on their profile (shown as ?). Hold on to that: missing values will matter in lesson 3.
Check the first hard constraint. Chen and Jon are not authorized to work in the US, so no amount of other strengths can make them a valid answer.
Check the second hard constraint. Dara and Hugo do not know Go. Dara is otherwise a superb match: close, active, Kubernetes, 10 years.
Six candidates survive both checks: Ana, Ben, Eli, Femi, Gita and Ines. This is the feasible set. Ranking only ever happens inside it.

blocks.md:
There are two tempting shortcuts, and both fail.

1. **Score everything.** Give each requirement a weight and add the points, including the must-haves. Then a candidate who is strong on many preferences can outscore a candidate who meets every requirement.
2. **Filter everything.** Treat every requirement as a yes or no test. Then the list is either empty (nobody satisfies all of them) or unordered, because a yes or no test gives every survivor the same standing.

blocks.prompt: Score everything: suppose work authorization and Go each add 2 points, and the preferences add up to at most 7.5 points (the weighted soft score you will build in lesson 4). Ana scores 11.5. Who do you expect in places 2 and 3?
blocks.reveal: Chen and Dara, tied at 9.5. Chen is not authorized to work in the US and Dara does not know Go, but each is perfect on every preference (7.5 points) and gets 2 points from the one hard requirement they do meet. Ines, the best *feasible* candidate after Ana, sits at 8.99. A weighted sum cannot express "never": it only says "usually worse".

blocks.title: Scoring everything lets infeasible candidates rise

scenes.caption: One weighted sum over all requirements, with 2 points each for work authorization and Go. Scores are computed with the lesson 4 formula plus those 4 points.
Red bars break a must-have. Chen and Dara take places 2 and 3. Hugo and Jon land last only because their preference scores happen to be low.

blocks.md:
Constraint satisfaction gives the right vocabulary. A **constraint satisfaction problem** (CSP) has variables, a domain of values for each, and constraints; a solution is an assignment that satisfies *every* constraint ([CS188 notes on CSPs](https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/csp/csps.html)). Russell and Norvig's textbook adds **preference constraints**: rules that say which valid solutions are better, without making any solution invalid. A CSP with preferences becomes a **constraint optimization problem** (COP).

Search maps onto this directly. **Hard constraints** decide membership in the feasible set. **Soft constraints** (preferences) become a score that orders the feasible set.

blocks.tex: \text{results} = \operatorname{sort}_{\downarrow s}\{\, d : h_1(d) \wedge \dots \wedge h_m(d) \,\},\quad s(d) = \sum_j w_j\, f_j(d)
blocks.caption: Hard constraints h_i are yes or no tests that select documents. Soft features f_j, each scaled to a comparable range, are weighted by w_j and summed only for the survivors.

blocks.md: Hard constraints decide **who is in**; soft constraints decide **the order**. Never let a preference buy its way past a requirement, and never let a preference silently remove someone.

blocks.title: The shape of a constrained ranking pipeline

scenes.caption: The query and the index meet at the hard filters, which output the feasible set: 6 of our 10 candidates.
Only the feasible set is scored by soft preferences (lessons 2 to 4).
Some rules apply to the list as a whole, such as a representation requirement in the top results. They run after scoring (lesson 5).
If the filters leave too few candidates, the system relaxes a constraint and asks again, and says so to the user (lesson 5).

blocks.question: A product team wants "must be authorized to work in the US" to be strongly preferred, so they give it a weight of 50 in a weighted sum where other features add at most 7.5. What is still wrong?
options: Nothing: a weight of 50 is equivalent to a filter
Unauthorized candidates still appear in the list whenever there are not enough authorized ones above them to push them off the page
The weight is too small; it must be infinite to be correct
Weighted sums cannot handle boolean features
blocks.explain: A large weight makes the ordering lexicographic (every authorized candidate outranks every unauthorized one), but it does not remove anyone. With few authorized matches, unauthorized candidates fill the remaining slots. That is exactly the right behavior for a relaxable preference (lesson 5) and exactly the wrong one for a legal requirement.

blocks.question: Which requirement is the best candidate for a soft constraint rather than a hard filter?
options: Candidate has the security clearance the contract legally requires
Candidate has not opted out of being contacted by recruiters
Candidate profile is in the recruiter's licensed country
Candidate lives within commuting distance of the office
blocks.explain: Distance is a matter of degree: 12 km is a bit worse than 3 km, not a disqualification. Legal, contractual and consent rules are binary and must never be traded for other strengths, so they belong in hard filters.

lessons.title: Elasticsearch bool: filter context versus query context

blocks.md:
Elasticsearch (and its fork OpenSearch) expresses this split with the `bool` query, which has four clause types ([Elasticsearch bool docs](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/query-languages/query-dsl/query-dsl-bool-query)):

- `must`: the document must match, and the clause **adds to the score**.
- `filter`: the document must match, but the clause's score **is ignored**.
- `should`: optional matches that **add to the score**.
- `must_not`: the document must not match; scoring is ignored.

The docs say the bool query takes a "more-matches-is-better" approach: the scores of every matching `must` and `should` clause are added together to form `_score`.

`filter` and `must_not` run in **filter context**. A filter answers a yes or no question, does no score calculation, and Elasticsearch automatically caches frequently used filters, so they run faster and use less CPU than scored queries ([query and filter context](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/query-languages/query-dsl/query-filter-context)). The docs recommend filters for structured fields: keywords, numbers, dates, booleans and geo points. `must` and `should` run in **query context** and their results are not cached.

That makes `filter` the natural home for hard constraints and `should` the natural home for preferences.

blocks.caption: Hard constraints in filter, preferences in should. Each constant_score clause scores exactly its boost when it matches.

blocks.md:
Two details from the docs decide how this query behaves:

1. **minimum_should_match default.** If the bool query has at least one `should` clause and no `must` or `filter` clause, the default is 1. Otherwise it is 0. Our query has filters, so the should clauses are purely optional: they reorder, they never exclude.
2. **Filter-only scores are zero.** A bool query with only `filter` clauses returns every match with `_score` 0. Adding `must: match_all` or wrapping the filter in `constant_score` gives every match 1.0 instead.

scenes.caption: The filter clauses admit the six feasible candidates. With only filters, every hit gets _score 0: the list has no meaningful order.
Add the Kubernetes should clause (boost 1.5). Ana, Eli and Gita gain 1.5 points each. Nobody is removed.
Add the 8+ years clause (boost 1.0). Scores of matching should clauses are summed: Ana now has 2.5 and Femi 1.0.
The result has ties: Eli and Gita at 1.5, Ines and Ben at 0. Yes or no preferences cannot tell a 3 km commute from an 18 km one. Lesson 3 fixes that.

blocks.md: A `should` clause is not an OR filter when the query also has a `filter` or `must` clause, because minimum_should_match then defaults to 0. Putting a hard requirement in `should` silently turns it into a mere preference. Set `minimum_should_match` explicitly if you need at least one of several options to match.

OpenSearch documents the same semantics: `filter` is a logical AND that does not affect the score and whose results are generally cached, `must_not` is excluded from scoring, and the minimum_should_match default is 0 when a `must` or `filter` clause is present ([OpenSearch bool docs](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/query-dsl/compound/bool/)).

blocks.question: An engineer writes `bool: { filter: [work_auth US], should: [skills go, skills rust] }` meaning "authorized AND (Go OR Rust)". What does the query actually return?
options: Authorized candidates who know Go or Rust
Authorized candidates, with Go and Rust only raising the score; candidates with neither are still returned
Nothing, because should requires all clauses to match
Candidates who know Go or Rust, whether authorized or not
blocks.explain: Because a filter clause is present, minimum_should_match defaults to 0 and the should clauses are optional. Fix it with "minimum_should_match": 1, or move a nested bool with the two should clauses into the filter list.

blocks.question: A recruiter types the free-text phrase `distributed systems` and also selects the facet location = New York. Where should each go?
options: Both in filter, for caching
Both in must, so both affect the score
The phrase in must (its text relevance should rank results), the location facet in filter
The phrase in filter, the location in should
blocks.explain: Text relevance is graded, so the phrase belongs in query context, where BM25 contributes to the score. A selected facet is a yes or no requirement on a structured field: filter context, no scoring work, and cacheable.

lessons.title: Decay functions turn distance and recency into smooth scores

blocks.md:
Preferences such as "close to the office" and "recently active" are about *how far* a value is from an ideal. A range filter draws a box: 24.9 km passes, 25.1 km fails. The Elasticsearch docs describe decay functions as "similar to a range query, but with smooth edges instead of boxes" ([function_score docs](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/query-languages/query-dsl/query-dsl-function-score-query)).

A decay function works on a numeric, date or geo point field and takes four parameters:

- `origin`: the ideal value (the office location, or `now` for dates, which is the default for date fields).
- `offset`: a distance around the origin that still scores a full 1.0. Default 0.
- `scale`: the distance beyond the offset at which the score has fallen to `decay`.
- `decay`: the score at distance `scale`. Default 0.5.

Write $d = \max(0, |v - \text{origin}| - \text{offset})$ for how far a value $v$ is outside the full-score zone. Elasticsearch offers three shapes. The formulas are copied from the docs; each one picks its constant so that the score equals `decay` when $d$ equals `scale`.

blocks.caption: Elasticsearch decay functions, as written in the function_score reference.

blocks.md:
Substituting the constants gives forms that are easier to compute by hand:

- gauss: $\text{decay}^{(d/\text{scale})^2}$
- exp: $\text{decay}^{d/\text{scale}}$
- linear: $\max(0,\ 1 - d(1-\text{decay})/\text{scale})$

Our distance preference uses gauss with origin at the office, offset 5 km, scale 20 km, decay 0.5. Ben lives 18 km away: $d = 13$, so Ben's score is $0.5^{(13/20)^2} = 0.5^{0.4225} = 0.746$.

blocks.title: Three decay shapes with origin 0, offset 5 km, scale 20 km

curves.label: linear
curves.expr: max(0, 1 - max(0, x - offset) * (1 - decay) / scale)

scenes.caption: Gauss alone: flat at 1.0 up to the 5 km offset, a gentle shoulder, then a fast fall. At offset + scale = 25 km it reaches exactly 0.5.
All three cross 0.5 at 25 km, because each is calibrated to hit decay at distance scale. They differ in the tails: exp keeps a long tail, linear hits zero.
Linear reaches 0 at d = scale / (1 - decay). With decay 0.5 that is twice the scale: 40 km beyond the offset, so 45 km from the office.
Raise the offset to 15 km: everyone within 15 km now scores 1.0. Offset is how you say "anything under this is equally good".
Lower decay to 0.25 with the original offset: the score at 25 km is now 0.25, so the same scale expresses a stricter preference.

blocks.title: Decay scores for the six feasible candidates

scenes.caption: Distance: gauss with offset 5 km, scale 20 km, decay 0.5. Ana (3 km) is inside the offset and scores 1. Gita at 60 km scores 0.005.
Ines has no location. The docs say that if the field is missing, the decay function returns 1, so Ines gets a perfect distance score.
Recency: gauss on the last-active date with origin now, offset 7 days, scale 30 days, decay 0.5. Ben (40 days) drops to 0.432.
Femi was last active 120 days ago: d = 113 days, so gauss gives 0.5 raised to (113/30) squared, about 0.00005. Rounded, zero.

blocks.md: A missing field scores **1**, the best possible decay value, in both Elasticsearch and OpenSearch. Profiles with no location beat everyone who lives a few kilometers away. Decide explicitly: require the field with an `exists` filter, index a default value, or accept the behavior on purpose.

blocks.prompt: Femi is 113 days past the recency offset (scale 30, decay 0.5). Estimate the gauss, exp and linear scores. Which shape keeps an old-but-strong candidate in contention?
blocks.reveal: Gauss: $0.5^{(113/30)^2} \approx 0.00005$. Exp: $0.5^{113/30} \approx 0.073$. Linear: $1 - 113 \cdot 0.5/30 < 0$, clamped to 0. Only **exp** keeps a long tail. Gauss is gentle near the origin but almost a cliff far away; linear is a hard cutoff in disguise.

blocks.question: With gauss on distance, offset 5 km, scale 20 km, decay 0.5: what does a candidate 25 km away score, and what does one 4 km away score?
blocks.explain: At 25 km, d = 25 - 5 = 20 = scale, so the score equals decay, 0.5. At 4 km the candidate is inside the offset, d = 0, so the score is 1.0.

blocks.question: A job board wants postings older than 60 days to stop getting any freshness credit, with a smooth decline before that. Which decay setup does that directly?
options: gauss with scale 60d
exp with scale 30d, decay 0.5
linear with origin now, scale 30d, decay 0.5
gauss with offset 60d
blocks.explain: Linear reaches exactly zero at d = scale / (1 - decay) = 30 / 0.5 = 60 days. Gauss and exp approach zero but never reach it, and an offset of 60 days would give full credit up to 60 days instead of none after it.

lessons.title: Weighting soft scores with function_score and phased ranking

blocks.md:
Elasticsearch combines several soft signals with `function_score`. It wraps a query (here, our filters) and applies a list of functions. Each function can have its own `filter`, so it applies only to matching documents, and a `weight` that multiplies its output. If `weight` is given with no other function, it simply returns the weight: that is how a yes or no preference becomes a fixed bonus.

Two settings combine the pieces ([function_score docs](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/query-languages/query-dsl/query-dsl-function-score-query)):

- `score_mode`: how function outputs combine: `multiply` (the default), `sum`, `avg`, `first`, `max` or `min`.
- `boost_mode`: how that result combines with the query score: `multiply` (default), `replace`, `sum`, `avg`, `max` or `min`.

blocks.caption: Hard constraints as non-scoring filters; four weighted soft functions summed. Our toy pool uses precomputed distances in place of geo math.
Decay scores lie in [0, 1], so the weights directly state how much each preference can be worth at most: 7.5 points in total.

blocks.title: Weighted contribution of each soft feature

scenes.caption: Each cell is weight times feature score from lesson 3. Ana is perfect on everything: 7.5, the maximum.
Ines is second only because the missing location scored 1, worth the full 3 distance points.
Eli and Gita lose distance points (35 km and 60 km) but Kubernetes and recent activity keep them in the middle.
Femi is close and senior but inactive for 120 days, so recency contributes nothing. Ben is mediocre on everything and ranks last.

blocks.title: Final soft scores, before and after fixing the missing location

scenes.caption: Ranking by the sum: Ana 7.5, Ines 4.99, Eli 4.12, Femi 3.95, Gita 3.52, Ben 3.10. Unlike lesson 2, there are no ties.
If an unknown location should count as far rather than perfect, Ines loses all 3 distance points and drops from second to last at 1.99.

blocks.prompt: Suppose we switch `score_mode` from `sum` to `multiply` and drop the two yes or no bonuses. Which candidate collapses most, and why does that matter?
blocks.reveal: Femi: the recency score is about 0.00005, and a product with a near-zero factor is near zero, however close and senior Femi is. Gita is next (distance factor 0.005). With `multiply`, any one bad feature acts like a veto, which quietly turns soft preferences back into near-hard constraints. `sum` keeps preferences compensatory: strength on one can make up for weakness on another.

blocks.md:
Weights are product decisions in this toy. In production they are usually learned: the soft features become inputs to a learning-to-rank model, as in the previous course on ranking features. The split stays the same.

LinkedIn Recruiter, as described by [Ramanath et al. (CIKM 2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.06473), first retrieves a candidate set of a few thousand members out of hundreds of millions, using the hard filters from the query and the selected facets (skill, title, industry), on LinkedIn's Galene search platform. A first-pass model scores those, then a second-pass service re-scores them with a gradient boosted tree or deep model and returns the top results.

Vespa makes the same separation explicit. The YQL `where` clause selects documents, and ranking features are computed only for the documents that match it. A rank profile then defines a **first-phase** expression, evaluated for every retrieved hit, so it must be cheap, and an optional **second-phase** expression that re-ranks the best hits: by default the top 100 per content node, adjustable with `total-rerank-count` ([Vespa phased ranking](https://docs.vespa.ai/en/ranking/phased-ranking.html)). `rank-score-drop-limit` can drop first-phase hits below a score threshold. Vespa's ranking intro builds a recency decay by hand as `pow(decay_const, doc_age_seconds / 3600)` ([ranking intro](https://docs.vespa.ai/en/ranking/ranking-intro.html)).

blocks.title: Filters first, cheap score next, expensive score last

scenes.caption: Filters cut the corpus to the feasible set. No scoring work is spent on documents that can never be shown.
The first phase scores every match with a cheap expression, such as our weighted decay sum.
Only the best N go to the expensive model: Vespa's default is 100 per content node. More work per document as the set shrinks.

blocks.question: In our function_score query, what is the effect of `"boost_mode": "replace"`?
options: The final score is the combined function score; the wrapped query's score is ignored
The filters are replaced by the functions
Each function's weight replaces its own output
Missing fields are replaced by the origin
blocks.explain: boost_mode decides how the function result combines with the query score; replace uses only the function score. Here the wrapped query is filter-only and scores 0, so the default multiply would make every final score 0.

blocks.question: Which change keeps the ranking from depending on how many kilometers apart two candidates within 5 km are?
options: Increase the distance weight
Use exp instead of gauss
It already does not: inside the 5 km offset every candidate scores 1.0
Set decay to 0.99
blocks.explain: The offset defines a zone around the origin with full score. Ana at 3 km and anyone at 1 km both get 1.0 for distance, which is what "anything within 5 km is fine" means.

lessons.title: Too few results: relaxation ladders and post-hoc constraints

blocks.md:
Now the recruiter tightens the search: within 10 km, active in the last 30 days, and 8+ years, all as hard filters, on top of work authorization and Go. Over-constrained queries are common, and an empty or one-item result page is a failure from the user's point of view.

A **relaxation ladder** is an ordered list of hard constraints that the system may downgrade to soft preferences, one rung at a time, until enough results come back. Elasticsearch has no built-in ladder; the application runs the query, checks `hits.total`, and re-issues it with fewer filters.

blocks.title: Results left at each rung of the relaxation ladder

scenes.caption: With all five hard filters, only Ana survives. One result.
Downgrade recency to a soft preference (it already has a decay function). Femi comes back: 2 results.
Downgrade distance. Still 2: among feasible candidates only Ana and Femi have 8+ years, so this rung was not the binding constraint.
Downgrade 8+ years. All six feasible candidates return, ordered by the lesson 4 soft score. Authorization and Go never moved.

blocks.md:
Rules that make a ladder trustworthy:

1. **Some constraints never relax.** Legal, consent and contractual rules stay hard on every rung.
2. **The order is a product decision**, ideally the user's own priority order. Rung 3 above added nobody, which shows that order matters and that the binding constraint is not always the obvious one.
3. **Relaxed constraints become soft, not deleted.** Candidates who meet them still rank higher.
4. **Tell the user** which constraint was relaxed, so a short list is never silently padded.

blocks.caption: An application-side ladder. Each rung removes one filter from the hard set; the soft functions still reward candidates who meet it.

blocks.md: A single-query alternative is to move the relaxable constraints into soft functions with a **dominant weight**: larger than everything else the soft score can add. Our soft score is at most 7.5, so a weight of 10 per relaxable constraint makes the ordering lexicographic: candidates who satisfy more relaxable constraints always come first, and the decay sum breaks ties within each level. This always returns results, at the cost of one more expensive query instead of a ladder of cheap ones.

blocks.prompt: Give each of the three relaxable constraints (active 30 days, within 10 km, 8+ years) weight 10 on top of the soft score. Predict the new order of the six feasible candidates.
blocks.reveal: Ana 37.5 (meets all three), Femi 23.95 (within 10 km and 8+ years), then Ines 14.99, Eli 14.12, Gita 13.52 (each meets only the recency constraint), and Ben 3.10 (meets none). Femi jumps from fourth to second because Femi satisfies two of the recruiter's stated requirements; within the one-constraint level, the old soft score still decides.

blocks.md: Some constraints apply to the **whole list**, not to one document, so no filter can express them. Fairness-aware re-ranking is the best documented example. [Geyik, Ambler and Kenthapadi (KDD 2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.01989) require that for every prefix of length $k$, each attribute value $a_i$ (such as a gender) appears at least $\lfloor p_{a_i} k \rfloor$ times and at most $\lceil p_{a_i} k \rceil$ times, where $p_{a_i}$ is the desired proportion.

blocks.tex: \forall k,\ \forall a_i:\quad \lfloor p_{a_i}\, k \rfloor \;\le\; \text{count}_k(a_i) \;\le\; \lceil p_{a_i}\, k \rceil
blocks.caption: The lower bound (minimum representation) is the one the paper calls more important for fairness.

blocks.md: Their **DetGreedy** algorithm builds the list position by position. If some attribute value is below its minimum, it takes the best remaining candidate among those values. Otherwise it takes the best remaining candidate among values that are still below their maximum. Below, our six feasible candidates carry an abstract group label X or Y; 2 of 6 are in X, so the desired proportions are 1/3 and 2/3, mirroring the paper's choice of the qualified pool's distribution.

blocks.title: DetGreedy re-ranks the soft-score order with p(X) = 1/3

scenes.caption: Score order puts both X candidates at positions 4 and 6. At k = 3 the minimum for X is floor(3/3) = 1, but the top 3 contain none.
k = 1 and k = 2: no group is below its minimum (floor(1/3) and floor(2/3) are 0 for X), so DetGreedy takes the best scores: Ana, then Ines.
k = 3: X is below its minimum of 1, so DetGreedy takes the best remaining X candidate, Femi (3.95), ahead of Eli (4.12).
k = 4 and 5: both groups are at or above their minimum and below their maximum, so the best scores win again: Eli, then Gita.
k = 6: X needs floor(6/3) = 2 and has 1, so Ben is taken. One swap was enough; every other position follows the score.

blocks.md: LinkedIn deployed DetGreedy in Recruiter, setting the desired gender distribution for each search to the distribution among candidates who qualify for that search's criteria. In a three-week A/B test in 2018, the share of queries with representative results rose from 33% to 95%, with no statistically significant change in InMails sent or accepted, and the re-ranker was ramped to 100% of Recruiter users. The authors chose post-processing partly because it is agnostic to the ranking model and fits where other business rules are already applied before display.

Three layers, three tools: per-document requirements are **filters**, per-document preferences are a **weighted score**, and requirements on the list as a whole are a **re-ranking pass**. When filters starve the list, relax in a declared order, keep the non-negotiables hard, and say what you relaxed.

blocks.question: In the DetGreedy example, suppose Femi's score were 4.50 instead of 3.95. What would change?
options: Femi would move to position 1
Nothing in the DetGreedy list: Femi is still placed at position 3, now with no score loss since Femi already outscores Eli
Ben would be placed at position 3
The list would violate the minimum for Y
blocks.explain: At k = 1 and 2 both groups are below their maximum, so the best scores win: Ana 7.5, Ines 4.99. Femi 4.50 then ranks ahead of Eli on score alone at k = 3, so the minimum for X is met without any forced swap.

blocks.question: A ladder relaxes `within 10 km` before `8+ years`, and the first rung adds no results. What does that tell you?
options: Distance was not the binding constraint for this query; the remaining hard filters exclude the same people anyway
The ladder is broken and should be reversed automatically
The index is missing location data
Relaxation should stop because results cannot grow
blocks.explain: Relaxing one constraint only helps if it was the one excluding candidates. Here everyone the relaxed rung would let back in also fails 8+ years, so the next rung is where the count changes. Logging which rung added hits helps tune the order.

blocks.question: Why can't a minimum-representation rule be written as a bool filter?
options: Filters cannot test keyword fields
Filters are cached, so they cannot change per query
It can: put the protected attribute in must_not
It is a property of the ranked list prefixes, not of any single document, so whether a document belongs at position k depends on the documents above it
blocks.explain: A filter decides each document independently. The rule "at least floor(p k) of group X in the top k" depends on positions and on the other documents, so it needs a pass over the scored list.
